**The Ring of Keys**

When my grandmother died, she left me a ring of keys. Nineteen of them, brass and steel and one small green one made of something that wasn't metal. There was no note. The lawyer shrugged and said the will just read: *To Ines, the keys.*

I knew the house key, which was the first thing I tried, and it was the only one that fit anything in that house. The rest were strangers. I tried the shed, the cellar, the cedar chest at the foot of her bed, the tin box in the pantry. Nothing. For a week I carried the ring in my coat pocket, and it clinked against my phone like a small, insistent question.

On the eighth day I gave up being sensible and took the keys into town.

Puerto Alto is not big. It has one main street, a church with a crooked bell, a bakery, a hardware store, and a pharmacy that still weighs things on a brass scale. I stood on the corner and thought: she lived here eighty-one years. Somewhere in these few blocks are nineteen locks.

I started with the hardware store because Mr. Varga had known her longest. He looked at the ring over his glasses and laughed, a short, surprised sound.

"She never told you?" he said. "Come around the back."

Behind the store was a green door I had walked past a thousand times as a child without seeing it. The second-largest key, the steel one with a worn head, turned as if it had been waiting. Inside was a narrow room with a workbench, a lamp, and shelves of jars. Each jar held broken things: a watch face, a doll's arm, a chipped teacup handle, a wedding ring bent almost flat.

"She fixed things," Mr. Varga said. "People brought them to her, and she'd keep them here until she figured out how. Some took years. She said a thing wasn't finished being broken until you understood how it broke."

"Why the secret? Why not just a shop?"

He picked up the bent ring and turned it in the light. "Because if it was a shop, people would pay her. And then they'd want it done by Thursday."

I stayed an hour. Then I took the ring and went looking for the next lock.

The brass key with the square bow opened a cabinet in the back of the church, behind the hymnals. Inside were forty or fifty umbrellas, all black, all slightly different. Father Almeida blushed when I found him. "For funerals," he said. "When it rains and someone comes without one. Your grandmother started collecting them in the seventies. She said nobody should stand in weather at a graveside and be *also* embarrassed."

The long thin key opened a mailbox at the post office, box 12, which had been rented in her name since 1968. Inside were letters, hundreds, bundled by year. They weren't addressed to her. They were addressed to no one, or to *Whoever Finds This*, or *To the Person at the Bakery Who Was Kind*. The postmistress, Delia, said people had been dropping them into the slot for decades, and my grandmother had let them pile up because no one else knew where unsent things should go.

"She read them?"

"Never. She said they weren't for reading. They were for having somewhere to be."

I sat on the post office steps a long time with that.

By the fifth day of walking I had opened eleven doors. A bench in the plaza had a locked compartment underneath, full of blankets and canned food, refreshed weekly by someone who never said who. A drawer at the pharmacy held a small fund in an envelope, labeled *for when they can't*. A cellar door under the bakery led to a room where a wall of shelves held jars of preserved apricots, each labeled with a name and a date. The baker, a big soft man named Tomás, cried openly when I asked. "Every person who lost someone," he said, "she'd bring them a jar the following summer. From the tree behind their own house, if they had one. She'd ask them nothing. She'd just leave it on the step."

I found that I had begun to walk differently, more slowly, looking at the town as if the buildings had their sleeves rolled up. Every shuttered window might be hiding something tender. It was like learning that a stranger's quiet face has been carrying something heavy for years.

That left eight keys. The small green one I saved for last, because I had a feeling about it.

Nobody could tell me what it opened. Mr. Varga didn't know. Delia didn't. Tomás said maybe it was a joke. I walked home in the late afternoon with the light going amber and my feet aching, and I stood in my grandmother's kitchen thinking that I had been foolish, that I was chasing a dead woman's shadow around a small town.

Then I noticed the clock.

It hung above the stove, a plain round thing she'd never fixed, though she fixed everything else. It had been stopped at 4:10 for as long as I could remember. I had always assumed it was broken. But there, in the base of its case, almost hidden by dust, was a keyhole the size of a grain of rice.

The green key slid in and turned. The back of the clock swung open, and inside, folded small, was a piece of paper in her cramped handwriting.

*Ines,*

*If you're reading this, you walked the whole town. Good. I hoped you would. I couldn't tell you outright, because you'd have thought it was about me, and it isn't. Every lock was somebody's need, and every key was somebody's trust. I didn't own any of it. I only held it.*

*The clock is stopped at ten past four because that's when your grandfather died. I could never bring myself to fix it. One broken thing I let stay broken. I think a person is allowed one.*

*The keys are yours now. You don't have to do any of it. But you might find, as I did, that being trusted with small secret kindnesses is the best way to belong to a place.*

*The apricot tree is ready in June.*

I read it three times. Then I put the note back, and for a while I just stood there while the kitchen went blue around me.

In June I made the jars. I didn't know how, so I asked Tomás, who showed me with his enormous gentle hands. I left the first one on the step of a woman whose husband had died in March. She never said anything. But the following week, there was a stopped watch on my doorstep with a sticky note that read simply: *When you have time.*

I opened the green door behind the hardware store, turned on the lamp, and sat down at the bench.
